title: This Once-Loved Growth Stock Is Down Hard From Its Highs -- Is Duolingo the Best Bargain of 2026?
content:
Key Points

Duolingo stock has fallen 80% from its May 2025 peak, creating a potential buying opportunity. AI translation tools still can't replace actual language learning for serious real-world use. The stock trades at just 12.5 times earnings despite 35% revenue growth and a 40% profit margin.10 stocks we like better than Duolingo ›

Language-learning pioneer Duolingo(NASDAQ: DUOL) was a hot ticket a year ago. On May 14, 2025, the stock had tripled in 52 weeks. The green owl could do no wrong.

But that turned out to be Duolingo's all-time peak, followed by a grueling downturn. Amid the rise of so-called vibe coding and the DeepSeek large language model (LLM), Duolingo investors saw new AI-powered threats. At the same time, Duolingo's management said it would prioritize user growth over profits for a while. That sounded scary to many profit-craving investors.

Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue »

As of April 22, 2026, the stock has lost 80% of its May 2025 value. And if you're a long-term investor, it just might be the best bargain on the market today.

The Babelfish is still fiction, folks

First and foremost, I don't think AI tools will replace language learning anytime soon.

I'm a natural-born Swede who learned English as a second language. Key helpers along the way included The Lord of the Rings, Bruce Springsteen's lyrics, and Swedish subtitles on American TV shows. Still, the English language has been my day job for the last 20 years, and I do translation as a side gig.

So I've done the heavy lifting to become bilingual, and I get paid to deliver natural-sounding language where today's best AI models can't. Sure, Google Translate or DeepL can provide a starting point for human revision, but no doctor, patent lawyer, or serious business would leave its mission-critical translations to AI tools. LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude are even worse. The next time you run across nonsensical instructions in a Temu gadget's manual, you can assume that an AI translation system did most of the damage.

And I sure wouldn't be where I am today if I had to run every thought through Google Translate. The helpful Babelfish of Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy is pure fiction in 2026.

The green owl has AI tricks of its own

In other words, there's still a place for language-learning tools, even if AI platforms are getting better all the time. Moreover, Duolingo is expanding its digital instruction platform to other fields, already including subjects such as math, music, and chess. The recently launched chess course has more than 7 million daily users, even though Duolingo doesn't even show up when you search the mobile app stores for "chess."

At the same time, Duolingo uses AI to explain your mistakes and drive simple conversations in the super-premium Max subscription. Wall Street thinks AI is killing the company, but Duolingo actually benefits from AI systems.

Image source: Getty Images.

Bargain-bin prices for a 40% profit margin? Yes, please.

That hasn't stopped Wall Street from overreacting to the perceived AI threat. You already saw the deep stock price dip. These days, Duolingo trades at just 12.5 times trailing earnings and 13.4 times free cash flows.

Those are bargain-bin ratios, usually reserved for slow-growing and mature business giants or companies on the brink of bankruptcy. Duolingo is neither of those things, sporting a 40% net profit margin while growing revenue by 35% year over year in Q4 2025.

I don't mind picking up Duolingo shares on the cheap while many investors lose sleep over the AI threat.

title: Duolingo in running to test migrant English skills for Home Office
content:
Duolingo is known for its free smartphone app that provides language courses - Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images

Duolingo is lining up to run migrant English language tests for the Home Office, The Telegraph can reveal.

The US app is closing in on a five-year, £816m contract to conduct language tests for foreign workers, students and other migrants seeking entry to Britain.

The Home Office has been assessing initial bids and will undertake technical assessments of companies in May. Best and final offers from companies in the running are expected over the summer and the Home Office plans to award the contract by November.

Duolingo is among the bidders for the lucrative contract, though there is no guarantee it will win the work.

Foreign visa applicants currently sit exams overseas with trained invigilators to prove they have a minimum level of English language skill.

Labour has been seeking to scrap the current system and replace it with an all-digital testing programme. Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, has also sought to strengthen entry requirements by demanding higher levels of English from migrants.Shabana Mahmood has sought to strengthen entry requirements by demanding higher levels of English from migrants - Leon Neal/Getty Images

Duolingo, known for its free smartphone app that provides language courses, has offered standardised online English testing since 2014.

Its timed tests gained popularity during the pandemic as assessment centres shut down. They are already being used by some UK universities as part of their applications process for foreign students.

While universities are allowed to set their own English tests for potential students, Duolingo is not currently approved for the “secure English language test”, the Home Office’s main immigration assessment.

Ms Mahmood’s plans to scrap the current in-person language testing system and make it online-only have attracted criticism from established providers, who warned of the risk of widespread cheating.

The International English Language Testing System (IELTS) consortium, which handles more than two thirds of UK assessments, wrote to Ms Mahmood in March to warn that online tests would result in “weaker security and more opportunities for malpractice” in the immigration system.

Challenges of remote testing

IELTS, a consortium made up of the British Council, Cambridge University Press & Assessment and education company IDP, dropped out of the bidding for the new online contract last month over its concerns about the plan.

“Evidence from research and regulatory practice shows that fully remote testing presents challenges in meeting these standards consistently – especially in the highest stakes environments where security is paramount,” the IELTS board said.

The group has warned that applicants could use AI to cheat the tests. Fraudsters could also use the technology to impersonate candidates, it added.

Story Continues

Duolingo has introduced ID checks for its language tests and uses eye tracking to check if students are trying to use crib sheets or AI.

Winning the Home Office contract would be a boost for Duolingo. Shares in the company, known for its green owl mascot, have collapsed 70pc in 12 months over concerns that new AI-powered language apps and translation services could hurt its user numbers.

Duolingo said in November that more than 50 million people globally were using its app each day.

In response to a parliamentary question this week on whether officials had held talks with Duolingo about the testing scheme, Mike Tapp, the immigration minister, said: “Prior to the Home Office English language testing programme publishing invitation to tender, five rounds of market engagement were conducted under non-disclosure agreements.

“However, there were opportunities for those who participated to share information that they wished for the Home Office to consider and ask clarifying questions.

“It would not be appropriate to disclose details of individual organisations’ participation in a confidential market engagement process.”

A government spokesman said: “The Home Office English language test is in live procurement and has not yet been awarded.”

A Duolingo spokesman declined to comment.

A Discounted Cash Flow, or DCF, model estimates what a company could be worth today by projecting its future cash flows and then discounting those back to the present using a required return.

For Duolingo, the model used is a 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to Equity approach. The latest twelve month Free Cash Flow stands at about $360.00 million.
